schema_faq_before: What is a screw identifier?

A screw identifier helps you narrow down what kind of fastener you have by matching visible features—head shape, drive recess, and optionally whether you expect metric or imperial threads—before you measure diameter and pitch.
How do I identify a screw?

First identify the head style and drive pattern visually, then measure major thread diameter and pitch or TPI. Use BoltLab’s Interactive Screw Identifier for the visual step, then the Thread Identifier tool with your measurements.
What is the difference between Phillips and Pozidriv?
Both are cross-shaped recesses. Pozidriv has extra shallow radial ticks between the main blades and requires a Pozidriv bit; it usually resists cam-out better than Phillips when paired correctly.
Can I identify thread size visually?

You cannot reliably tell thread diameter or pitch from appearance alone. Visual ID narrows the fastener family; you still need calipers and a pitch gauge or thread identifier for the thread specification.

schema_faq_before: ¿En qué se diferencian los sujetadores métricos de los imperiales?

Los métricos usan milímetros para diámetro y paso de rosca (p. ej. M8 x 1.25). Los imperiales usan diámetros en pulgadas y roscas por pulgada TPI (p. ej. 5/16-18 UNC). No son intercambiables sin conversión.
¿Cuándo conviene métrico y cuándo imperial?
Métrico en vehículos modernos y maquinaria ISO. Imperial en equipos norteamericanos antiguos y cuando el plano indica UNC/UNF.
¿Puedo sustituir un perno métrico por uno imperial?
No sin comprobar diámetro y paso. Las tallas casi iguales pueden destrozar roscas o fallar. Use una tabla o herramienta de conversión para hallar equivalentes correctos.

schema_faq_before: ¿Qué es el paso de rosca?
Es la distancia entre dos crestas de rosca consecutivas, medida según el eje. En métrico se da en mm; en imperial suele usarse TPI (roscas por pulgada).
¿En qué se diferencian rosca gruesa y fina?
La gruesa tiene mayor paso (menos hilos por longitud), adecuada para materiales blandos y montaje rápido. La fina tiene menor paso, mejor para paredes finas y ajuste fino.
¿Cómo convierto paso de rosca a TPI?
TPI = 25,4 dividido por el paso en mm. Use nuestro convertidor de paso a TPI para el cálculo al instante.

schema_faq_before: What is the difference between a bolt and a screw?
Bolts typically pass through unthreaded holes and use a nut; screws often engage a pre-tapped hole or form their own thread. Load direction and head design also differ.
Can I use a bolt without a nut?
Only if the hole is threaded (then it acts like a screw). In unthreaded holes, the nut (or threaded counterpart) is required for the joint.
Do bolts and screws use the same thread sizes?
Yes. Metric and imperial thread sizes (e.g. M6, 1/4-20) apply to both bolts and screws. Use our size chart or converters to match sizes.

schema_faq_before: What is the difference between metric and imperial fasteners?

Metric fasteners use millimeters for diameter and thread pitch (e.g. M8 x 1.25). Imperial fasteners use inch-based diameters and threads per inch (e.g. 5/16-18 UNC). They are not interchangeable without conversion.
When should I use metric vs imperial bolts?
Use metric for most modern vehicles and ISO-standard machinery. Use imperial for legacy North American equipment and when drawings specify UNC/UNF.
Can I substitute a metric bolt for an imperial one?
Do not substitute without checking diameter and pitch. Near-match sizes can strip threads or fail. Use a conversion chart or tool to find correct equivalents.

schema_faq_before: What is tap drill size?
Tap drill size is the diameter of the hole you drill before tapping. It is smaller than the bolt major diameter so that the tap can form threads; typically chosen for about 75% thread depth.
How do you calculate tap drill size for metric?
A common rule is: tap drill diameter = major diameter minus pitch. For M6 x 1.0, drill = 6 - 1 = 5 mm. Use our Tap Drill Calculator for exact values.
What if I drill the hole too large?
Oversized holes give shallow threads and weak engagement. Use the recommended tap drill size from a chart or our calculator for reliable threads.

schema_faq_before: What are the main parts of a screw?

Most machine-style screws include a head (bearing and drive), an unthreaded shank (if present), a threaded section that engages the nut or tapped hole, and often a point. Head style and drive are separate from thread specification.
What is the difference between the shank and the thread?
The shank is the smooth cylindrical section under the head. The thread is the helical ridge that provides axial load and engagement. Fully threaded fasteners may have little or no unthreaded shank.
How do I measure screw size?
Measure major diameter across the thread crests and measure pitch (metric) or threads per inch (imperial). Use BoltLab’s Thread Identifier once you have those measurements.
Is the head the same as the drive?
No. The head is the load-bearing region and may be hex, pan, countersunk, etc. The drive is the recess or external wrenching feature used to apply torque—Phillips, Torx, hex socket, and so on.
When does the point style matter?
Point style affects starting, centering, and whether the fastener drills or cuts its own hole—important for self-tapping and self-drilling types versus standard machine screws.

schema_faq_before: What is the difference between Phillips and Pozidriv?
Pozidriv has extra shallow radial ticks between the main cross blades, reducing cam-out versus Phillips when used with the correct bit.
Torx vs hex socket: which handles more torque?
Both are high-torque internal drives. Torx (hexalobular) spreads load over six lobes; hex sockets rely on six flat walls—both beat Phillips for torque if bits fit well.
What is a Robertson drive?
Robertson is a square recess common in Canada and woodworking. It resists cam-out and centers the bit well.
How do I identify my screw thread after the drive?
Measure major diameter and pitch (or TPI), then use BoltLab’s Thread Identifier tool.

schema_faq_before: What is the difference between head type and head profile?
Head type names the style (e.g. pan, hex). Head profile is the overall silhouette—how tall, wide, and flush vs. proud the head looks relative to the workpiece.
What does a countersunk head look like in profile?

schema_faq_before: What is a thread type?

Thread type names the thread family and series—such as ISO metric coarse, metric fine, UNC, or UNF—defined by diameter, pitch or threads per inch, and flank angle. It is separate from head style or drive.
What is the difference between UNC and UNF?

Both are unified inch threads. UNC is coarse pitch (fewer threads per inch); UNF is fine pitch (more threads per inch) for the same nominal diameter, offering different strength and engagement characteristics.
When should I use metric coarse vs fine?
Coarse (e.g. M6 × 1) is the default for general assembly. Fine pitches reduce vibration loosening and allow finer adjustment where specified—always match the mating part or standard.
How do I identify my thread type?
Measure major diameter and pitch in millimeters or TPI, note 60° flank angle for common metric and unified threads, then compare to a chart or use BoltLab’s Thread Identifier.
What is the difference between thread type and screw drive?
Thread type defines helical engagement along the shank. Drive type (Phillips, Torx, etc.) only defines how torque is applied at the head.
